code.title: Functions as first-class objects

followUps: Any object whose class defines __call__ is callable, not just functions. Classes are callable (calling one builds an instance), bound methods, built-ins like len, functools.partial objects and instances of your own class with __call__ all work. Use callable(x) to test. Example: class Adder: def __init__(self, n): self.n = n; def __call__(self, x): return x + self.n, so Adder(3)(4) returns 7. Lambdas are just anonymous functions.

__defaults__ is a tuple holding the default values of the parameters, and those values are evaluated once, when def runs, not on each call. That is why a mutable default such as def f(x, acc=[]) is shared between calls: the same list lives in f.__defaults__. Calling f(1) then f(2) gives [1] then [1, 2]. Use None as the default and create the list inside the function.

code.title: LEGB lookup and UnboundLocalError

followUps: No. Only functions, classes and modules create scopes in Python; if, for, while and with blocks do not. A name assigned inside a loop or an if stays alive after the block ends. After for i in range(3): pass, i is 2. (Comprehensions are the exception: they have their own scope, so their loop variable does not leak.) If the loop never ran, reading i would raise NameError.

Because a class body is not an enclosing scope for the functions defined inside it. Name lookup skips the class namespace, so a method must write self.rate or Cls.rate. Example: with class A: rate = 2; def f(self): return rate, calling f raises NameError unless a global rate exists. The class body runs once as its own temporary namespace, and its names become attributes of the class, found through the instance or class.

code.title: Closure cells and late binding
code.python:
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc

a, b = make_counter(), make_counter()
print("a:", a(), a(), "b:", b())          # independent cells
print("freevars:", a.__code__.co_freevars)
print("cell value:", a.__closure__[0].cell_contents)

# Late binding: closures capture variables, not values
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print("late binding:", [f() for f in funcs])

# Fix: bind the current value as a default argument
fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print("fixed:", [f() for f in fixed])

followUps: Bind the current value when the lambda is created, using a default argument (lambda i=i: i) or functools.partial. Without that, every lambda reads the same variable i after the loop ends, so [lambda: i for i in range(3)] returns [2, 2, 2]. With lambda i=i: i each function stores its own value and returns [0, 1, 2]. A factory function that takes i as a parameter also works, since each call makes a new cell.

Prefer a class when the state is more than one or two values, when you need several operations on that state (reset, get, set), when you want to inspect or test the state, or when it must be pickled. A closure is lighter for one small private piece of state, like a counter. Example: a counter that also needs reset() and value is clearer as a class with self.n. Closure state is hidden inside cells, which makes debugging harder.

code.title: global vs nonlocal
code.python:
total = 0
def add_global(x):
    global total          # rebind the module-level name
    total += x

def counter():
    count = 0
    def bump():
        nonlocal count    # rebind the enclosing function's name
        count += 1
        return count
    return bump

items = []
def mutate(x):
    items.append(x)       # mutation needs neither keyword

add_global(5); add_global(2)
print("total:", total)
c = counter()
print("counter:", c(), c(), c())
mutate(1); mutate(2)
print("items:", items)

def level1():
    x = "level1"
    def level2():
        x = "level2"
        def level3():
            nonlocal x
            x = "changed"
        level3()
        return x
    return level2(), x
print("nearest wins:", level1())

followUps: It binds to the nearest enclosing function scope that defines x and ignores the outer one. If f sets x, and inside it g sets x, and inside g a function h uses nonlocal x, then h changes g's x and f's x stays the same. Lookup goes from the inside out and stops at the first match, so only one level is ever rebound.

Because any function can change it, so a test's result depends on what ran before it, and tests stop being independent. A function using a global counter returns 1 on the first test and 2 on the second. You must reset state between tests, and running tests in parallel or in random order can break them. Passing values as arguments and returning results (or injecting an object) keeps the function predictable and easy to test.

code.title: *args, **kwargs and parameter order

followUps: They force callers to name the argument, which makes calls readable and lets you add parameters later without breaking old code. Compare connect(host, 5432, True) with connect(host, port=5432, ssl=True): the second says what each value means. Put them after * or *args: def connect(host, *, port=80, ssl=False). Passing connect(h, 443) then raises TypeError, which prevents swapped-argument bugs for flags.

It lets you name a parameter privately, so callers cannot pass it by keyword and you can rename it later without breaking anyone. Parameters before / are positional-only: def f(x, /). It also lets **kwargs accept a key with the same name, such as def f(self, /, **kw) with f(self=1). Built-ins use it: len(obj=[]) fails because len's argument is positional-only.

code.title: Writing a decorator: import time vs call time

followUps: The decorated function silently returns None, because the wrapper runs the original but throws away its result. With wrapper ending in func(*args, **kwargs) and no return, add(2, 3) prints nothing useful and gives None, and later code like add(2, 3) + 1 raises TypeError. Always write return func(*args, **kwargs). Also return wrapper from the decorator itself, or the name becomes None.

Make the wrapper an async def and await the original, otherwise you only get the coroutine object back without running the timing or logging around the real work. Example: async def wrapper(*a, **k): start = time.time(); r = await func(*a, **k); log(time.time() - start); return r. If you used a plain wrapper, the timer would stop immediately, measuring about 0 seconds instead of the real wait. Still apply functools.wraps.

code.title: What functools.wraps copies

followUps: Call the original through __wrapped__, which wraps sets on the wrapper: func.__wrapped__(args) or inspect.unwrap(func). A test can then check the core logic without the decorator's retry, cache or logging. Example: if @retry wraps fetch, then fetch.__wrapped__(url) runs one plain attempt. This only works if the decorator used functools.wraps.

No. The wrapper runs exactly the same code; wraps only copies metadata (name, docstring, annotations, module, __dict__) and adds __wrapped__ once at decoration time. Calling cost and results are unchanged. The one subtle effect is that tools that read metadata, such as inspect.signature, now report the original's signature, which can mislead you if the wrapper changes the arguments it accepts.

code.title: Decorator factory with optional parentheses

followUps: With the three-level version, @retry without parentheses passes the function as times, so retry(func) returns the inner decorator function instead of a wrapped one. Your function name now refers to decorator, and calling fetch() fails with TypeError (missing the function argument). You must write @retry(). The optional-parentheses design fixes this by checking whether the first argument is callable or None.

A bare raise re-raises the same exception with its original traceback, so you can see where the real failure happened. Writing raise Exception('failed') loses the type (callers catching ValueError would miss it) and hides the cause. If you do need a new type, use raise RetryError(...) from e, which keeps the chain. A bare raise is only valid inside an except block.

code.title: lru_cache: hits, misses, eviction, pitfalls

followUps: The standard lru_cache has no expiry, so add one yourself: store (value, time) in a dict and recompute if too old, or pass a changing extra argument such as int(time.time() // 60) as part of the key so each minute gets a fresh entry. Example: get(x, now=int(time.time()//60)) caches for at most 60 seconds. Simpler still is calling f.cache_clear() on a timer. Remember that a TTL cache is no longer a pure function.

Use a dict plus a doubly linked list, so both lookup and move-to-front are O(1). On get, find the node in the dict, unlink it and put it at the head. On put, insert at the head; if size exceeds capacity, remove the tail node and its dict key. In Python, collections.OrderedDict does it: d.move_to_end(k) on a hit and d.popitem(last=False) on overflow. Space is O(capacity).

code.title: partial vs lambda
code.python:
import functools, pickle

def power(base, exp):
    return base ** exp

square = functools.partial(power, exp=2)
cube = functools.partial(power, exp=3)
print("square(5) =", square(5), "| cube(2) =", cube(2))
print("introspect:", square.func.__name__, square.args, square.keywords)
print("override:", square(3, exp=4))        # call keyword wins

# lambda in a loop: late binding bug
lams = [lambda x: power(x, e) for e in (1, 2, 3)]
pars = [functools.partial(power, exp=e) for e in (1, 2, 3)]
print("lambdas:", [f(2) for f in lams])
print("partials:", [f(2) for f in pars])

# partial pickles (function must be importable), lambda does not
print("pickle partial:", len(pickle.dumps(square)) > 0)
try:
    pickle.dumps(lambda x: x)
except Exception as e:
    print("lambda pickle fails:", type(e).__name__)

followUps: Use a keyword for it, or a lambda. partial only fills positional arguments from the left, so for def f(a, b, c) use partial(f, c=10) only for the last, or write lambda a, c: f(a, 5, c) to fix the middle one. With f(a, b), partial(f, b=2) freezes the second by name. That is the standard trick, and it works because keyword arguments can be frozen in any position.

partialmethod is the same idea for methods in a class body: it makes a new method with some arguments frozen, and still receives self properly. Example: inside a class, set_on = partialmethod(set_state, True) creates obj.set_on() that calls obj.set_state(True). A plain partial in a class body would not bind self, because partial objects are not descriptors.

code.title: functools.reduce: use and avoid
code.python:
from functools import reduce
from math import gcd
import operator

nums = [12, 18, 24]
print("gcd of", nums, "=", reduce(gcd, nums))
print("product:", reduce(operator.mul, [1, 2, 3, 4], 1))

# initial value protects the empty case
try:
    reduce(operator.add, [])
except TypeError as e:
    print("empty without initial:", e)
print("empty with initial:", reduce(operator.add, [], 0))

# merge dicts
dicts = [{"a": 1}, {"b": 2}, {"a": 9}]
print("merged:", reduce(lambda acc, d: {**acc, **d}, dicts, {}))

# Better built-ins when they exist
print("sum is clearer:", sum(nums), "== reduce:", reduce(operator.add, nums))

# trace the accumulator
steps = []
reduce(lambda acc, x: steps.append((acc, x)) or acc + x, [1, 2, 3])
print("acc, x pairs:", steps)

followUps: Fold the list of functions into one, applying them right to left: compose(f, g)(x) means f(g(x)). Code: def compose(*fns): return lambda x: reduce(lambda acc, f: f(acc), reversed(fns), x). With compose(str, abs)(-5) the value goes -5, then 5, then '5'. For left-to-right order drop reversed. Cost is O(n) calls for n functions.

No. reduce is eager: it consumes the whole iterable immediately and returns one final value, unlike map or filter, which return lazy iterators. If you want to see every intermediate result lazily, use itertools.accumulate: list(accumulate([1, 2, 3, 4])) gives [1, 3, 6, 10], while reduce(add, [1,2,3,4]) gives only 10.

code.title: Class-based decorator and the missing self

followUps: The descriptor protocol is how attribute access can run code: if a class attribute has a __get__(self, instance, owner) method, then obj.attr calls it and uses its result. Functions are descriptors, and that is how obj.method becomes a bound method with obj filled in as self. Adding __set__ or __delete__ makes it a data descriptor, which takes priority over the instance dict. property is built on it.

Put @property and @staticmethod on the outside, and your own decorator directly on the plain function, so each sees what it expects. Example: @property above @my_deco above def x(self) works. Reversed, my_deco receives a property object, not a function, and breaks (functools.wraps fails or you lose self). Decorators apply bottom-up, so the one closest to def sees the raw function.

code.title: Typing decorators with ParamSpec
code.python:
import functools
import time
from typing import Callable, TypeVar, ParamSpec

P = ParamSpec("P")
R = TypeVar("R")

def timer(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R]:
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        result = func(*args, **kwargs)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
        print("  %s took %s" % (func.__name__, "fast" if elapsed < 1 else "slow"))
        return result
    return wrapper

@timer
def add(a: int, b: int = 0) -> int:
    return a + b

print("add(2, b=3) =", add(2, b=3))
print("annotations kept:", add.__annotations__)
print("P is", type(P).__name__, "| R is", type(R).__name__)
# A type checker now rejects add("x", b=1.5) because P keeps (a: int, b: int)
print("wrapped name:", add.__name__)

followUps: Concatenate says that a decorator adds one or more fixed parameters in front of the original's parameters. Callable[Concatenate[Request, P], R] means the function takes a Request first, then whatever P is. Use it for decorators that inject something, like a database connection or request: the wrapper takes (*args, **kwargs) and passes the extra first argument itself, so callers see the shorter signature.

An untyped decorator returns something like Callable[..., Any] or Any, so the editor loses the real parameter names, types and return type of the function. You get no completion for arguments, no tooltips, and no error when you call add('x') wrongly. After the decorator, hover shows (...) -> Any. Using ParamSpec keeps the original signature, so autocomplete and type checking continue to work.
